title: Bald Range wildfire, Summerland, British Columbia (August 2026)
story: On the evening of August 7, 2026 a wildfire started in the hills west of Summerland, in British Columbia's Okanagan valley. After a long drought, strong westerly winds pushed it downhill towards Okanagan Lake: about 5,000 ha burned in three hours and 15,600 ha by August 10. More than 20,000 people in Summerland and Peachland were ordered to leave, an 80-year-old woman died while evacuating, and about 150 structures were damaged or destroyed; in Faulder only 8 of 81 homes survived. The fire was held on August 28 at about 25,200 ha. NISAR's L-band radar sees through the smoke and into the forest canopy.
method: The HV radar channel measures the forest canopy: the wave bounces in needles and branches. For every pixel we compare HV after the fire with July 25 (before), and remove the common change of the unburned forest 1 to 6 km around the fire (rain, calibration). In that unburned forest HV moves by about 0.6 dB on its own, so a drop of 1 dB (2 times) marks canopy loss and 2 dB (3 times) severe canopy loss, on land that was vegetated before and in patches of 9 or more pixels. The result is checked against the official fire perimeter and the Sentinel-2 burn severity.
limitations: Provisional NISAR data (calibrated, not yet officially validated). The radar sees the canopy: light ground fires under a canopy that survived are not detected. NISAR has no data between July 27 and August 10, so the first days of the fire are not imaged. Rain on August 30 and partial coverage in October add noise. Logging also lowers HV; it is told apart by the date and the official perimeter.
satellite: NISAR (NASA-ISRO), L-band, track 71 descending, frame 63, HV channel
sources: NISAR L2 GCOV, Provisional (NISAR_L2_GCOV_PROVISIONAL_V1), NASA Earthdata / ASF
BC Wildfire Service fire perimeter K51490, BC Data Catalogue (PROT_CURRENT_FIRE_POLYS_SP)
Sentinel-2 L2A photos and burn severity (ESA Copernicus), via Earth Search
BC Wildfire Service, Bald Range incident K51490; Castanet, Summerland Review, Kelowna Capital News, CBC News and The Canadian Press (August to October 2026)

stages.headline: Before: the forests above Summerland

metric.label: last NISAR pass before the fire started

stages.summary: On July 25, after weeks of drought, the forests west of Summerland are bright in the radar's HV channel: the wave bounces many times in needles and branches before coming back. Lakes, rock and bare ground are dark. This is the reference image: the next NISAR pass came on August 18, after the fire had started, because NISAR has no data between July 27 and August 10.

labels.lowEnd: -25 dB: dark, water, rock or bare ground

stages.headline: During the fire: the canopy echo collapses

metric.label: of canopy already lost inside the fire perimeter on August 18

stages.summary: On August 18, eleven days after ignition, the fire was still burning (about 22,000 ha) while most of Summerland was allowed back home. The radar echo of the forest had dropped clearly over 41 km² inside the fire perimeter. We compare each pixel with July 25 and remove what the unburned forest around the fire did on its own (rain, season), so only the change caused by the fire remains. Yellow: canopy loss; red: severe canopy loss.

stages.headline: After: where the forest canopy burned

metric.label: of forest canopy lost by September 11, 90% of it inside the official perimeter

stages.summary: Once the fire was held, NISAR shows 83 km² of lost canopy, 29 km² of it severe. An independent optical check agrees: the radar flags 82% of the areas Sentinel-2 rates as high burn severity and only 2% of unburned land. Light ground fires under a surviving canopy are not seen: the radar answers where the forest canopy burned.

actions: Map canopy loss with NISAR while a fire is still burning: radar sees through the smoke that blinds optical satellites.
Start erosion and debris-flow checks on the slopes with severe canopy loss (red) above Summerland, whose drinking-water source was damaged.
Inside the official perimeter, areas without canopy loss likely burned lightly: use them to plan surveys and replanting.
